bibl.title: High-Entropy Metal Diborides: A New Class of High-Entropy Materials and a New Type of Ultrahigh Temperature Ceramics

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: seven equimolar five-component metal diborides, and whether each forms a single high-entropy solid-solution phase
span.quote: To synthesize high-entropy metal diborides, five commercial metal diboride powders of equimolar amounts were mixed and mechanically alloyed via high energy ball milling (HEBM) for six hours; subsequently, the HEBM powders were compacted into disks of 20-mm diameter and densified utilizing spark plasmas sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 minutes under a pressure of 30 MPa.

span.label: whether high-entropy solid solutions form in a non-cubic layered ceramic, and whether the inherited size-difference criterion predicts which compositions do
span.quote: Prior studies suggested, mostly based on empirical observations, that a necessary (but not sufficient) criterion for forming a single-phase (disordered) HEA is that the computed δ of the solid solution should be sufficiently small: δ ≤ δmax ≈ 4% or 4.3%.

span.label: the first crystalline high-entropy non-oxide ceramics, and a size-difference measurand recomputed from lattice constants rather than atomic radii
span.quote: This work has greatly extended the knowledge of high-entropy materials, not only since it is the first time crystalline high-entropy non-oxide ceramics (specifically borides) have been synthesized, but also because these high-entropy metal diborides exhibit a unique layered hexagonal crystal structure with alternating rigid two-dimensional (2D) boron nets and high-entropy 2D layers of metal cations (as essentially a class of quasi-2D high-entropy materials), as schematically shown in Fig. 1, which distinctly differs from any other high-entropy crystalline phases reported to date.

span.label: existence
span.quote: To synthesize high-entropy metal diborides, five commercial metal diboride powders of equimolar amounts were mixed and mechanically alloyed via high energy ball milling (HEBM) for six hours; subsequently, the HEBM powders were compacted into disks of 20-mm diameter and densified utilizing spark plasmas sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 minutes under a pressure of 30 MPa.

span.label: entropy stabilisation of a single solid-solution phase against decomposition into separate compounds
span.quote: In an HEA, the configurational entropy of a solid-solution phase is maximized to stabilize it against the formation of intermetallics. Typically, five or more elements can be mixed in a HEA in equimolar concentrations to produce a maximum molar configurational entropy of ΔSmix = RlnN, where N is the number of equimolar components and R is the gas constant.

span.label: high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering, characterised by XRD, SEM-EDX and aberration-corrected STEM
span.term: high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering, characterised by XRD, SEM-EDX and aberration-corrected STEM
span.quote: To synthesize high-entropy metal diborides, five commercial metal diboride powders of equimolar amounts were mixed and mechanically alloyed via high energy ball milling (HEBM) for six hours; subsequently, the HEBM powders were compacted into disks of 20-mm diameter and densified utilizing spark plasmas sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 minutes under a pressure of 30 MPa.

span.label: because Gibbs free energy is H minus TS, a phase with large S becomes more stable as temperature rises, so a maximally mixed solid solution can win over separate compounds at high temperature
span.quote: Since the minimization of Gibbs free energy (G = H−TS, where H is enthalpy, S is entropy, and T is temperature) dictates the thermodynamic stability of a material at a constant pressure, a high-entropy material (with large S) can be thermodynamically more stable (particularly) at high temperatures, motivating this study to explore the phase stability and fabrication feasibility of high-entropy metal diborides, as a new type of high-entropy materials as well as a new class of ultra-high temperature ceramics (UHTCs).

span.label: the rigid 2D boron net deforms the metal cations toward a strain-free spacing in the basal plane, which compresses the size differences along a and leaves the c-axis free to express them
span.quote: Interestingly, the computed δa values are small (in the range of 1.3% to 2.3% for all seven specimens) because the M-M bonds are strained by the rigid boron net (that can deform metal cations and M-M bond lengths towards an ideal “strain-free” value dictated by stronger B-B bonds; Fig. 1). Thus, the computed δc values may better represent the average size difference because of less constraint along the c-axis.

span.label: a small size difference is necessary but not essential, and a very small value is not a guarantee of a single high-entropy phase
span.quote: However, we should emphasize that small differences in lattice parameters (measured by small δaand δc) are only one necessary, but not essential, condition for forming high-entropy solutions. A very small δ value is certainly not a guarantee for forming a single-phase, high-entropy, solid solution.

span.label: size differences are not the only factors - mixing enthalpy and valence electron concentration may also decide whether a single phase forms
span.quote: Moreover, the average size differences are certainly not the only factors that determine the ability to form a single high-entropy phase. For example, it is known that an average lattice parameter a of ~3.04 Å would produce “strain-free” metal layers that match the rigid boron net, thereby being favored; this may also be a factor for HEB #7 to exhibit single high-entropy phase since its average a (of ~3.081 Å) has the closest match to the ideal strain-free value (Supplementary Table S-I; despite that this factor also favors HEB #6, where the largest δcmay be a determining factor). In addition to the several size factors discussed above, the mixing enthalpy, as well as the valence electron concentration, may also play an important role in determining whether a single high-entropy phase forms.

span.label: hardness and oxidation resistance are strongly affected by the porosity and oxide inclusions that this fabrication route introduces
span.quote: It is important to emphasize that both the hardness and oxidation resistance can be affected by the microstructure, e.g., the porosity and oxide inclusions, significantly. Thus, we choose to compare the high-entropy and individual metal diborides fabricated using the same method to allow a fair assessment of relative hardness and oxidation resistance (even if our specimens have high levels of porosity and oxidation inclusions due to HEBM than those fully-dense and oxide-free specimens prepared by other fabrication routes). We expect that fully-dense and oxide-free specimens should have higher hardness and better oxidation resistance.

span.label: whether these materials are good or bad for oxidation resistance has no simple answer, and systematic property investigation is outside this study
span.quote: This will be particularly important for improving oxidation resistance, which depends on many (often kinetic) factors; thus, there is perhaps no simple answer on whether high-entropy metal diborides are good or bad for oxidation resistance (and some other properties).

span.label: one of the seven compositions did not form a single phase, and the reason is not settled
span.quote: As the only special case, a secondary boride phase was observed in HEB #6, (Hf0.2Zr0.2W0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2, with XRD peaks matching those of the (Ti1.6W2.4)B4 compound, while the major XRD peaks still represent a hexagonal metal diboride solid-solution phase (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. S6).

span.label: the Hume-Rothery binary solid-solution size rule, carried from alloy metallurgy into multicomponent ceramics and then re-measured
span.quote: The original Hume-Rothery solid-solution rule suggests that (rsolute−rsolvent)/rsolvent ≤ 15% is one of the necessary conditions for forming a binary solid solution.

span.label: six individual metal diborides fabricated by the identical milling and sintering route, as the comparison group
span.note: eliminates: a high-entropy advantage produced by the fabrication route rather than by the composition, since the comparison specimens were milled and sintered identically · outcome: held
span.quote: To conduct a fair assessment of the relative performance of high-entropy and conventional metal diborides, we measured six single-phase high-entropy diborides, along with a controlled group of HfB2, ZrB2, TaB2, NbB2, TiB2, and CrB2 specimens made by the identical HEBM and SPS fabrication processing using the same processing parameters (except for CrB2; see “Methods” section for explanation).

span.label: porosity and oxide inclusion held constant between the high-entropy and conventional specimens rather than eliminated
span.note: eliminates: hardness and oxidation differences being attributed to composition when microstructure - porosity, oxide inclusions - affects both significantly · outcome: held
span.quote: It is important to emphasize that both the hardness and oxidation resistance can be affected by the microstructure, e.g., the porosity and oxide inclusions, significantly. Thus, we choose to compare the high-entropy and individual metal diborides fabricated using the same method to allow a fair assessment of relative hardness and oxidation resistance (even if our specimens have high levels of porosity and oxidation inclusions due to HEBM than those fully-dense and oxide-free specimens prepared by other fabrication routes). We expect that fully-dense and oxide-free specimens should have higher hardness and better oxidation resistance.

span.label: MoB2 excluded from the rule-of-mixtures average, with the direction of the resulting bias stated
span.note: eliminates: a rule-of-mixtures baseline inflated by a phase that is not an equilibrium bulk phase at the temperature in question · outcome: held
span.quote: Because MoB2 is not an equilibrium bulk phase below 1500 °C, the averages for HEB#2-HEB#5 that contains 20% MoB2 were calculated without MoB2. Yet, it is well established that MoB2 has a lower melting temperature and theoretical hardness than all the other metal diborides in HEB#2-HEB#5 (HfB2, ZrB2, TaB2, NbB2, and TiB2) so that the actual averages from the “rule of mixtures,” if we could make and measure MoB2 via the same procedure, should be even lower.

span.label: weight-change data outside the two temperature windows where the change exceeds measurement error
span.note: eliminates: measurement error masquerading as oxidation - the weights are reported only in the two temperature windows where the change is large enough to exceed it, and not outside them · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: We found the measured weights are generally accurate for the oxidization temperatures of 1000–1200 °C (from direct weighting of specimens) and for the annealing temperatures of 1400 and 1500 °C, where the weight changes were sufficiently large to allow to be weighted accurately in crucibles. Outside these two temperature windows, the weight gains/losses were typically on the same order of magnitude as the measurement errors; thus, those data are not reported.

span.label: HEA = typically five or more elements in equimolar concentration, giving maximum molar configurational entropy RlnN
span.quote: In an HEA, the configurational entropy of a solid-solution phase is maximized to stabilize it against the formation of intermetallics. Typically, five or more elements can be mixed in a HEA in equimolar concentrations to produce a maximum molar configurational entropy of ΔSmix = RlnN, where N is the number of equimolar components and R is the gas constant.

span.label: 'high-entropy material' HAS A CONTESTED SCOPE - glasses count only 'in a broad definition', said in parentheses
span.quote: Most prior studies of crystalline high-entropy materials have been conducted for metallic HEAs of mostly simple face- and body-centered cubic (FCC and BCC), as well as occasionally hexagonal close packing (HCP), crystal structures; much less studies have been done for making crystalline high-entropy ceramics (albeit that glasses can be considered high-entropy materials in a broad definition), particularly those with more complex, non-cubic, crystal structures.

span.label: delta <= 4% or 4.3% = a NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT criterion, and it is empirical, not derived
span.quote: Prior studies suggested, mostly based on empirical observations, that a necessary (but not sufficient) criterion for forming a single-phase (disordered) HEA is that the computed δ of the solid solution should be sufficiently small: δ ≤ δmax ≈ 4% or 4.3%.

span.label: the same delta, recomputed from LATTICE CONSTANTS instead of atomic radii, because no radius represents the real bond lengths
span.quote: In reality, metal diborides [M2+(B−)2] form a highly anisotropic layered structure (i.e., the hexagonal AlB2 structure), where each metal atom donates two electrons and the M-B bonds (between the metal and B layers) have mixed ionic and covalent characteristics (see Fig. 1). Within the 2D metal layers, M-M bonds are strained significantly by the more rigid boron net (Fig. 1). Thus, none of the available (metallic, covalent or ionic) radii can effectively represent the actual bond lengths in the metal diborides in the AlB2 structure (Fig. 1).

span.label: 'only one necessary, but not essential, condition' - the authors' own hedge on their replacement
span.quote: However, we should emphasize that small differences in lattice parameters (measured by small δaand δc) are only one necessary, but not essential, condition for forming high-entropy solutions. A very small δ value is certainly not a guarantee for forming a single-phase, high-entropy, solid solution.

span.label: delta-c is the discriminating one and delta-a is not, because the boron net constrains the a-axis
span.quote: Interestingly, the computed δa values are small (in the range of 1.3% to 2.3% for all seven specimens) because the M-M bonds are strained by the rigid boron net (that can deform metal cations and M-M bond lengths towards an ideal “strain-free” value dictated by stronger B-B bonds; Fig. 1). Thus, the computed δc values may better represent the average size difference because of less constraint along the c-axis.

span.label: contradicts → the delta <= 4% size-difference criterion for forming a single-phase high-entropy solid solution
span.note: HEB #7 has delta about 8%, double the stated maximum, and forms a single high-entropy phase anyway - so the criterion fails as a NECESSARY condition, which is the only thing it was ever claimed to be
span.quote: By simply plugging the values of metallic or covalent radii of the metals, and the computed δ values are in the range of 3.5% to ~8% (Table S-I in the Supplementary Material); specifically, HEB #7 has the highest δ ≈ 8%; yet, it still forms single-phase, high-entropy, solid solution.

span.label: extends → Rost et al.'s entropy-stabilized oxide, the only previously reported crystalline high-entropy ceramic
span.note: extends the class from oxides to borides and from cubic to layered hexagonal
span.quote: To the best of our knowledge, this class of entropy-stabilized oxides and its derivatives represent the first and only crystalline high-entropy ceramics that have been reported to date.

span.label: configurational entropy —causes→ solid-solution phase
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: In an HEA, the configurational entropy of a solid-solution phase is maximized to stabilize it against the formation of intermetallics. Typically, five or more elements can be mixed in a HEA in equimolar concentrations to produce a maximum molar configurational entropy of ΔSmix = RlnN, where N is the number of equimolar components and R is the gas constant.

span.label: entropy-stabilized oxides —distinct-from→ high-entropy metal diborides
span.note: differs in: crystal structure - cubic rocksalt against layered hexagonal, and oxide against boride · strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: To the best of our knowledge, this class of entropy-stabilized oxides and its derivatives represent the first and only crystalline high-entropy ceramics that have been reported to date.

span.label: boron nets —contrasted-with→ Hume-Rothery
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — the rigid net is why the inherited radius-based rule cannot be applied here as written
span.quote: In reality, metal diborides [M2+(B−)2] form a highly anisotropic layered structure (i.e., the hexagonal AlB2 structure), where each metal atom donates two electrons and the M-B bonds (between the metal and B layers) have mixed ionic and covalent characteristics (see Fig. 1). Within the 2D metal layers, M-M bonds are strained significantly by the more rigid boron net (Fig. 1). Thus, none of the available (metallic, covalent or ionic) radii can effectively represent the actual bond lengths in the metal diborides in the AlB2 structure (Fig. 1).

span.label: the inherited size-difference criterion fails: the specimen with the largest atomic-radius delta still forms a single high-entropy phase
span.quote: By simply plugging the values of metallic or covalent radii of the metals, and the computed δ values are in the range of 3.5% to ~8% (Table S-I in the Supplementary Material); specifically, HEB #7 has the highest δ ≈ 8%; yet, it still forms single-phase, high-entropy, solid solution.

span.label: delta computed from the c lattice constant separates the six single-phase specimens from the one that failed, where the atomic-radius delta does not
span.quote: Coincidentally, Specimens #1-#5 and #7, for which single-phase, high-entropy, solid solutions did form, all have computed δc values in the range of 3.9% to 5.2%, whereas HEB #6, for which single-phase did not form, has the largest computed δc value of ~6.2%.

span.label: a smaller delta-c appears to matter more than a smaller delta-a
span.quote: It is interesting to further note that HEB #7 (with a simple high-entropy phase) has a greater δabut smaller δcthan those of HEB #6 (with two boride phases), suggesting that a smaller δc may be more important than a smaller δa.

span.label: STEM imaging confirms 2D high-entropy metal layers with no layered segregation along the c-axis
span.quote: A careful digital image analysis (Fig. S11) revealed that the measured standard deviations of lattice spacings between the basal (0001) planes are only ~0.6% of the average measured c lattice parameter or the measured variations from STEM ABF and HAADF images are ~0.02 Å, which directly confirmed the formation 2-D high-entropy metal layers without a layered segregation of different metal specimens in different (0001) basal planes, where these 2-D metal layers are well separated by the rigid 2-D boron nets in between (Fig. 1).

span.label: hardness and oxidation resistance exceed the average of the individual diborides made the same way, with porosity working against them
span.quote: Initial property assessments indicated that both the hardness and the oxidation resistance of these high-entropy metal diborides are generally greater or better than the average performances of the individual (conventional) metal diborides made by the identical HEBM and SPS fabrication processing. We understand that both hardness and oxidation resistance should critically depend on microstructures; the presence of porosity and oxide inclusion, as a consequence of the HEBM procedure that we adopted for promoting the homogenization of high-entropy solid solutions, adversely affected the hardness and oxidation resistance.
